intro: Walk down your street. A mail carrier waves. A bus stops. A store opens its door. These people live and work near you. They are your community. This unit is about them.
First, the people. Who lives near you? Who has a job that helps you? What places do you share? And what happens when something breaks and no one can fix it alone?
Then, the money. Why do people work? What do they buy? Why can't you have everything? You will learn the difference between a need and a want, and what it feels like to save for something big.
bigQuestion: How do people in a community help each other get what they need?

timeline.t: The bus driver stops at your corner. You climb on.
Your teacher starts the day. That is her job.
You eat an apple. It grew on a farm far from here.
A swing is broken. The class tells the principal.
Sam trades grapes for crackers. Leo shares his sandwich.
The librarian reads a story to your class.
The mail carrier puts a letter in your box.
Your family buys milk, a need, and skips the candy, a want.
A grown-up comes home from work. She earned money today.
You drop a coin in your jar. You are saving up.

words.d: the people who live and work near each other
a person with a job that helps others
to work together to get something done
something you must have to live, like food or water
something you would like to have but can live without
to get money for work you do
work that someone does for you, like a haircut
to keep money now so you can use it later

choices: People who live and work near each other
test.why: A community is the people who live and work near each other.

test.q: Who cares for you when you are sick?
test.why: A nurse is a helper whose job is to care for sick or hurt people.

test.q: Which community has tall buildings and many streets?
test.why: A city is a big community. Chicago is a city.

test.q: The swing broke. How did the neighbors fix it?
choices: Each did a small part together
test.why: The neighbors cooperated. One brought a tool, one a chain, and others helped.
Shelter keeps you safe from cold and rain. You cannot live without it.
A video game is fun but you can live without it. That makes it a want.

test.q: Why do grown-ups go to work?
test.why: People work to earn money. Then they buy what they need.
A haircut is work someone does for you. That is a service.

test.q: Leo has eleven dollars. He wants a cone and a bike. What must he do?
test.why: Money runs out. Leo cannot buy everything, so he must choose.
Milk starts on a farm. A cow makes it. Then trucks carry it to the store.

write.prompt: Leo has eleven dollars. Should he buy the ice cream cone now or save for the bike? Say what he should do. Tell what you read about needs, wants and saving. Tell why your choice is best.
tips: Claim: say what Leo should do, the cone or the bike.
Evidence: is the cone a need or a want? Is the bike?
Reasoning: tell what Leo gives up with each choice.
The other side: say why someone might pick the other choice.

title: Our Community

chapters.title: Neighbors, Helpers and Jobs
chapters.bigQuestion: Who are the people in our community, and how do they help each other?

story.title: The Day We Fixed the Swing
story.kicker: One swing hangs by a single chain. A whole block shows up to fix it.
paragraphs: Rosa lives on a street in Chicago. Her favorite swing is at the park. One morning she runs to it. The swing hangs by one chain. The other chain is broken. Rosa cannot swing. She walks home sad.
Rosa tells her dad. Her dad tells Mr. Bell next door. Mr. Bell tells the mail carrier, Ms. Kim. Ms. Kim tells everyone on her route. By dinner, the whole block knows.

On Saturday, people come to the park. Mr. Bell brings a wrench. Ms. Kim brings a new chain. A nurse from the corner brings water for everyone. Rosa's class picks up trash. A firefighter on her day off holds the ladder.
By noon the swing has two chains. Rosa sits down. Her dad pushes. She flies up high. Every person did one small job. Together they fixed the swing.
story.think: Rosa could not fix the swing alone. Who helped? What did each person do?

lessons.title: People Near Each Other
lessons.mainIdea: A community is the people who live and work near each other.
reading: Look out your window. You see houses. You see a store. You see people walking. Those people are your *community*. A community is people who live and work near each other.
You live in a community. So does your teacher. So does the person at the store. You do not need to know every name. You share the same streets. You share the same park.
People in a community need each other. The baker sells bread. The bus driver drives the baker to work. You ride the same bus. Everyone helps in some way.

words.d: the people who live and work near each other

look.title: Rosa's Street
look.text: Look at Rosa's street. Mr. Bell waters his flowers. Ms. Kim carries a bag of mail. Two kids ride bikes. A bus stops at the corner. A man opens the store door. All of these people live or work here.
look.prompt: Who on Rosa's street is part of her community?

check.q: What is a community?
choices: People who live and work near each other
Only the people in your house
check.why: A community is the people who live and work near each other, like on Rosa's street.

check.q: Who is part of your community?
choices: The people on your streets, like the bus driver
check.why: People who share your streets and park are your community. The bus driver is one.

check.q: Why do people in a community need each other?
choices: They all have the same name
They do not need each other
Each one helps in some way
check.why: The baker sells bread. The bus driver drives. Everyone helps in some way.

lessons.title: City, Town and Country
lessons.mainIdea: Communities can be big cities, small towns or the open country.
reading: Some communities are big. A *city* has tall buildings. It has many streets. Many people live close together. Chicago is a city in Illinois.
Some communities are small. A *town* has a few streets. It has one school. People often know each other by name.
Some people live in the *country*. Houses are far apart. Farms and fields are all around. Neighbors may live a mile away. They are still a community. They still help each other.

words.d: a big community with many people and many streets
a small community with a few streets
land outside cities and towns, with farms and open fields

look.title: Three Windows
look.text: Look out three windows. Window one: a tall building and a busy street. Cars honk. Window two: a quiet street with a school at the end. Window three: a red barn and a field of corn. No other house in sight.
look.prompt: Which window shows a city? A town? The country? How do you know?

check.q: Which is a big community with tall buildings?
check.why: A city has tall buildings and many streets. Chicago is a city.

check.q: In the country, where are the houses?
choices: Stacked on top of each other
check.why: In the country, houses are far apart. Farms and fields are all around.

check.q: Neighbors in the country live a mile apart. Are they a community?
choices: No, they live too far away
Only if they have a school
Yes, they still help each other
check.why: A community is people who live near each other and help. Country neighbors do that too.

lessons.title: Helpers Who Keep Us Safe
lessons.mainIdea: Firefighters and nurses have jobs that keep people safe and well.
reading: A *firefighter* puts out fires. She wears a heavy coat. She drives a big red truck. She also helps when a car crashes. She teaches kids what to do in a fire.
A *nurse* helps sick people. He checks your ears. He gives you a shot. He puts a bandage on a cut. Nurses work in clinics and in schools.
These are community helpers. A *helper* has a job that helps others. Firefighters and nurses keep us safe and well. They are ready every day.

words.d: a person whose job is to put out fires and help in emergencies
a person whose job is to care for sick or hurt people
a person with a job that helps others

look.title: The School Nurse
look.text: Look at Jamal. He fell on the playground. His knee is bleeding. He walks to the nurse's room. The nurse washes the cut. She puts on a bandage. She gives him an ice pack. Jamal goes back to class.
look.prompt: What did the nurse do to help Jamal?

check.q: What does a firefighter do?
check.why: A firefighter puts out fires. She also helps at crashes and teaches fire safety.

check.q: Jamal cut his knee. Who helps him at school?
check.why: A nurse cares for sick or hurt people. The school nurse cleaned Jamal's cut.

check.q: What is a community helper?
choices: A person who is always sick
A person with a job that helps others
check.why: A helper has a job that helps others. Firefighters and nurses are helpers.

lessons.title: Helpers Who Bring and Carry
lessons.mainIdea: Mail carriers and bus drivers bring things and people where they need to go.
reading: A *mail carrier* walks the same streets each day. She carries a heavy bag. She puts letters in each mailbox. Rain or snow, she comes. A birthday card comes because of her.
A *bus driver* takes people places. He drives kids to school. He drives workers to their jobs. He stops at every corner. He waits for you to sit down.
Think about your day. Did a bus bring you to school? Did a letter come to your house? Helpers bring and carry. Without them, things would not get where they need to go.

words.d: a person whose job is to bring letters and packages to homes
a person whose job is to drive a bus and take people places

look.title: Ms. Kim's Route
look.text: Look at Ms. Kim. It is snowing. She wears boots and a warm hat. Her bag is full. She walks up to each house. Letter, letter, package. She waves to Rosa. At the last house, her bag is empty.
look.prompt: Why does Ms. Kim walk in the snow? What would happen if she stayed home?

check.q: What does a mail carrier do?
check.why: A mail carrier walks the streets and puts letters in each mailbox.

check.q: Who drives kids to school?
check.why: A bus driver takes people places. He drives kids to school and workers to jobs.

check.q: Ms. Kim stays home. What happens?
choices: The fire does not go out
check.why: Ms. Kim brings the mail. If she stays home, no letters reach the houses.

lessons.title: Every Job Matters
lessons.mainIdea: A librarian and a farmer help too, and every job in a community matters.
reading: A *librarian* works at the library. She helps you find a book. She reads stories out loud. She shows you how to use a computer. Books are free to borrow because of her.
A *farmer* grows food. He plants corn in spring. He picks it in fall. In Illinois, farmers grow lots of corn. Your cereal may come from an Illinois farm.
Some jobs are loud. Some are quiet. Some are far from town. Every job matters. Take away the farmer, and there is no food. Take away the librarian, and there are no books.

words.d: a person whose job is to help people find and use books
a person whose job is to grow food or raise animals

look.title: Take One Away
look.text: Look at a town. Now take away the farmer. The store has no corn. Take away the bus driver. Kids walk for miles. Take away the nurse. No one fixes a cut. Take away the librarian. The story time stops. Each job left a hole.
look.prompt: Pick one job. What happens to the town if no one does it?

check.q: Who helps you find a book?
check.why: A librarian works at the library. She helps you find books and reads stories.

check.q: What does a farmer do?
check.why: A farmer grows food. In Illinois, farmers grow lots of corn.

check.q: Why does every job matter?
choices: Each job fills a need that others have
check.why: Take away the farmer, and there is no food. Each job fills a need.

lessons.title: Places We Share
lessons.mainIdea: A community has places that everyone can use, like a park or a library.
reading: A community has special *places*. A school is a place to learn. A library is a place for books. A park is a place to play. A clinic is a place to see a nurse or doctor.
A store is a place to buy food. A place of worship is where some families pray. A church, a mosque, a temple, a synagogue. Each family may go to a different one.
Some places are shared by everyone. The park is for all. The library is for all. Rosa, Mr. Bell and Ms. Kim all use the same park. That is why they all fixed the swing.

words.d: a spot in a community made for something, like a park for playing
a place where a nurse or doctor helps sick people

look.title: Who Uses the Park?
look.cite: A count of Rosa's park on one Saturday (story)
look.prompt: Who uses the park the most? Who else uses it?

check.q: Where do you go to borrow a book?
check.why: A library is a place for books. You can borrow them for free.

check.q: A clinic is a place to do what?
check.why: A clinic is where a nurse or doctor helps sick people.

check.q: Why did so many people fix the swing?
choices: The park is shared by everyone
check.why: The park is for all. Rosa, Mr. Bell and Ms. Kim all use it, so they all helped.

lessons.title: Fixing a Problem Together
lessons.mainIdea: People in a community can solve a problem by each doing a small part.
reading: A *problem* is something wrong that needs fixing. The swing was broken. That was a problem. Rosa could not fix it alone. She was too small. She had no chain.
Rosa told her dad. Her dad told a neighbor. Soon many people knew. Each one asked, what can I do? One brought a tool. One brought a chain. One brought water.
This is how a community works. You do not fix a big problem alone. You *cooperate*. That means you work together. Each person does a small part. The big job gets done.

words.d: something wrong that needs to be fixed
to work together to get something done

look.title: The Messy Playground
look.text: Look at the school playground. Trash blows across the grass. Cups sit under the slide. A class sees it. One kid gets a bag. One kid gets gloves. Two kids pick up cups. One kid holds the bag open. In ten minutes, the grass is clean.
look.prompt: How did the class solve the trash problem? Could one kid do it alone in ten minutes?

check.q: What is a problem?
check.why: A problem is something wrong that needs fixing, like the broken swing.

check.q: What does cooperate mean?
check.why: To cooperate is to work together. Each person does a small part.

check.q: How did the class clean the playground so fast?
choices: One kid did all the work
The wind blew the trash away
Each kid did a small part
check.why: One got a bag, some picked up cups, one held the bag. Together it took ten minutes.

choices: People who live and work near each other
review.why: A community is the people who live and work near each other.

review.q: Which community has houses far apart and fields all around?
review.why: In the country, houses are far apart and farms are all around.

review.q: Who puts letters in your mailbox?
review.why: A mail carrier walks the streets and brings letters to each house.

choices: Cares for sick or hurt people
review.why: A nurse checks your ears, gives shots and bandages cuts.

review.q: Which place is for borrowing books?
review.why: A library is a place for books. A librarian helps you find them.

review.q: The swing was broken. How did it get fixed?
choices: Many people each did a small part
review.why: Neighbors cooperated. One brought a wrench, one a chain, and others helped too.

chapters.title: Needs, Wants and Money
chapters.bigQuestion: How do people get the things they need and the things they want?

story.title: Leo's Lemonade Stand
story.kicker: Leo wants a bike. He has one jar, a pitcher of lemonade and a hot Saturday.
paragraphs: Leo sees a red bike in the store window. He wants it. It costs a lot. Leo has two dollars in a jar. His mom says, you can earn more. So Leo makes a plan.
On Saturday, Leo sets up a table by the sidewalk. He makes lemonade. He makes a sign. Fifty cents a cup. The sun is hot. Neighbors stop by. Ms. Kim buys a cup. Mr. Bell buys two. The jar gets heavy.
At the end of the day, Leo counts. He has eleven dollars. He is thirsty and tired. He walks past the ice cream truck. He wants a cone. A cone costs two dollars.
Leo stops. If he buys the cone, the bike is farther away. If he saves, the bike is closer. He thinks hard. He puts the money back in the jar. The bike can wait, but not for long.
story.think: Leo had to choose: the cone now or the bike later. What would you choose? Why?

lessons.title: Things We Must Have
lessons.mainIdea: A need is something you must have to live, like food, water, shelter and clothes.
reading: Some things you must have. You must have food. You must have water. You must have a place to sleep. You must have clothes. These are *needs*.
A need is something you cannot live without. Without food, you get weak. Without water, you get sick. Without a home, you get cold and wet. A home is *shelter*.
Think about your day. You ate breakfast. You drank water. You put on clothes. You slept in a bed last night. You met your needs. Every person has the same four needs.

words.d: something you must have to live, like food or water
a place that keeps you safe from cold, rain and heat, like a home

look.title: The Rainy Night
look.text: Look at a family on a rainy night. They are inside. The roof keeps them dry. A pot of soup is on the stove. Each person has a warm sweater. There is a glass of water by each plate. Outside, the rain pours.
look.prompt: Find the four needs in the picture: food, water, shelter, clothes.

check.q: Which one is a need?
check.why: You cannot live without water. It is a need. A toy and candy are not.

check.q: What is shelter?
choices: A place that keeps you safe and dry
check.why: Shelter is a place like a home. It keeps you safe from cold, rain and heat.

check.q: What happens if a person has no food?
check.why: Food is a need. Without it, a person gets weak. That is why it is a need.

lessons.title: Things We Would Like
lessons.mainIdea: A want is something you would like to have but can live without.
reading: Leo wants a bike. He wants an ice cream cone. He can live without both. They are *wants*. A want is something you would like but do not need.
A toy is a want. A treat is a want. A video game is a want. Wants are fun. It is fine to have wants. But needs come first.
Sometimes it is tricky. Shoes are a need. Your feet must stay safe. A second pair with lights that blink? That is a want. You already have shoes.

words.d: something you would like to have but can live without

look.title: Sort the Bag
look.text: Look at a shopping bag. Inside: a loaf of bread, a bottle of water, a bag of gummy bears, a winter coat, a sticker book and a jug of milk. Some of these things keep you alive. Some are just fun.
look.prompt: Which things in the bag are needs? Which are wants?

check.q: What is a want?
choices: Something you would like but can live without
Something you must have to live
check.why: A want is something you would like. Leo can live without a bike, so it is a want.

check.q: Which one is a want?
check.why: A sticker book is fun but not needed. Bread and a coat are needs.

check.q: You have shoes. Blinking shoes are what?
choices: A need, because feet must be safe
Not a need or a want
A want, because you already have shoes
check.why: Shoes are a need. A second pair with lights is a want. Your feet are already safe.

lessons.title: Working to Earn
lessons.mainIdea: People work at jobs to earn money.
reading: Leo's mom goes to work. She is a nurse. At the end of the week, she gets paid. She *earns* money. To earn means to get money for work you do.
Almost every grown-up works to earn money. The bus driver earns money. The farmer earns money. The librarian earns money. Then they use it to buy what they need.
Leo worked too. He made lemonade. He sold it. He earned eleven dollars. Work first. Then money. That is how earning goes.

words.d: to get money for work you do
the coins and bills people use to buy things

look.title: Leo's Lemonade Day
look.prompt: When did Leo sell the most cups? Why do you think so?

check.q: What does earn mean?
choices: To get money for work you do
To find money on the ground
check.why: To earn is to get money for work. Leo's mom earns money as a nurse.

check.q: How did Leo earn eleven dollars?
choices: His mom gave it to him
He found it in the park
check.why: Leo worked. He made lemonade and sold it. That is earning.

check.q: Which comes first?
check.why: People do work first. Then they get paid. Work first, then money.

lessons.title: Goods and Services
lessons.mainIdea: Money buys goods, which are things, and services, which is work someone does for you.
reading: Money buys two kinds of things. The first kind is *goods*. Goods are things you can hold. A bike is a good. Bread is a good. A cup of lemonade is a good.
The second kind is *services*. A service is work someone does for you. A haircut is a service. A bus ride is a service. A doctor visit is a service. You pay for the work, not a thing.
Leo sold a good. The lemonade was a thing. Leo's mom sells a service. She cares for sick people. Both earn money. Both help others.

words.d: things people make or grow and sell, like bread or a bike
work that someone does for you, like a haircut

look.title: A Trip Downtown
look.text: Look at Leo and his mom on Saturday. They ride the bus. They buy a new pair of shoes. Leo gets a haircut. They buy two apples. On the way home, a man fixes a flat tire on the bus.
look.prompt: Which things they paid for were goods? Which were services?

check.q: What is a good?
choices: A thing you can hold, like bread
check.why: Goods are things you can hold. Bread, a bike and lemonade are goods.

check.q: Which one is a service?
check.why: A haircut is work someone does for you. You pay for the work, not a thing.

check.q: Leo's mom is a nurse. What does she sell?
check.why: A nurse does work for people. Caring for the sick is a service.

lessons.title: You Cannot Buy It All
lessons.mainIdea: Money runs out, so you must choose what to buy.
reading: Leo has eleven dollars. The bike costs more. The cone costs two dollars. He cannot have the cone and the bike. Money runs out. So Leo must *choose*.
Every person chooses. Your family chooses at the store. Milk or juice? New shoes or a new coat? No one can buy everything. There is never enough money for it all.
When you choose one thing, you give up another. Leo picks the bike. He gives up the cone. That is the cost of his choice. Think before you choose.

words.d: to pick one thing instead of another

look.title: Three Dollars
look.text: Look at Mia at the school fair. She has three dollars. A popcorn costs two dollars. A ring toss costs two dollars. A sticker costs one dollar. She can buy popcorn and a sticker. Or she can play ring toss and get a sticker. She cannot do all three.
look.prompt: What would you pick? What would you give up?

check.q: Why must Leo choose?
check.why: Leo has eleven dollars. He cannot buy both the cone and the bike.

check.q: Leo picks the bike. What does he give up?
check.why: When you choose one thing, you give up another. Leo gives up the cone.

check.q: Mia has three dollars. Can she buy all three things?
choices: No, she does not have enough
check.why: All three cost five dollars. Mia has three. She must choose.

lessons.title: Saving Up
lessons.mainIdea: Saving means keeping money now so you can buy something bigger later.
reading: Leo puts his money in the jar. He does not spend it. He is *saving*. To save means to keep money for later. Every dollar in the jar is a step toward the bike.
Saving is hard. You have to wait. The cone is right there. The bike is far away. But each week the jar gets fuller. One day it is enough.
Many people save. A family saves for a car. A grown-up saves for a trip. Some people keep money in a *bank*. A bank keeps money safe until you need it.

words.d: to keep money now so you can use it later
a place that keeps people's money safe

look.title: Leo's Jar, Week by Week
look.cite: Leo's savings chart on the fridge (story)
look.prompt: Does the jar go up or down each week? What is Leo doing?

check.q: What does save mean?
check.why: To save is to keep money now so you can use it later. Leo saves in a jar.

check.q: Why is saving hard?
check.why: The cone is right there. The bike is far away. Saving means waiting.

check.q: What does a bank do?
check.why: A bank is a place that keeps people's money safe until they need it.

lessons.title: Trading and Sharing
lessons.mainIdea: People can trade or share to get things without using money.
reading: You do not always need money. Sam has two apples. Ana has two cookies. Sam gives Ana an apple. Ana gives Sam a cookie. They *trade*. Each gets something new.
Long ago, most people traded. A farmer traded eggs for shoes. Today we mostly use money. But kids still trade cards. Neighbors still trade help.
You can also *share*. Leo shares his lemonade with his little sister. She pays nothing. Sharing is giving without getting. It makes a community stronger.

words.d: to give one thing and get another thing back
to let someone have or use something of yours

look.title: The Lunch Table
look.text: Look at the lunch table. Sam has grapes. Ana has crackers. Sam gives Ana some grapes. Ana gives Sam some crackers. Jae forgot his lunch. Leo gives Jae half his sandwich. Jae gives nothing back. Leo smiles anyway.
look.prompt: Who traded? Who shared? How can you tell the difference?

check.q: What is a trade?
choices: Giving one thing and getting another back
check.why: In a trade, each person gives something and gets something. Sam and Ana traded.

check.q: Leo gives Jae half his sandwich. Jae gives nothing back. What is that?
check.why: Sharing is giving without getting anything back. Leo shared.

check.q: Long ago, how did a farmer get shoes?
check.why: Long ago, most people traded. A farmer could trade eggs for shoes.

lessons.title: Farm to Store to Table
lessons.mainIdea: Food starts on a farm, travels to a store, and ends up on your table.
reading: Look at the milk on your table. Where did it come from? Not the store. The store is just one stop. Milk starts on a *farm*. A cow makes it. A farmer milks the cow.
Next a truck picks up the milk. It goes to a place that puts it in jugs. Another truck takes the jugs to the store. A worker puts them on a shelf.
Your family buys the milk. You bring it home. You pour it on your cereal. Farm, truck, store, table. Many workers helped. Each one earned money. Each one did a job.

words.d: a place where people grow food or raise animals

look.title: The Trip of a Corn Flake
look.text: Look at a field in Illinois. Corn grows tall. A farmer picks it with a big machine. A truck takes it to a factory. The factory makes flakes and puts them in a box. A truck takes the box to the store. Your family buys it. You eat it for breakfast.
look.prompt: Count the stops from field to bowl. Who did a job at each stop?

check.q: Where does milk start?
check.why: Milk starts on a farm. A cow makes it and a farmer milks the cow.

check.q: What carries milk from the farm to the store?
check.why: Trucks carry the milk to be put in jugs and then to the store.

check.q: How many workers help get milk to your table?
check.why: The farmer, the truck drivers and the store worker all did a job.

lessons.title: Food Is Work Too
lessons.mainIdea: Growing food is a job, and the food we buy pays the people who grew it.
reading: A farmer in Illinois plants corn in spring. All summer she waters and weeds. In fall she picks it. That is months of work. Then she sells the corn.
Your family pays for food at the store. Some of that money goes to the farmer. Some goes to the truck driver. Some goes to the store worker. Buying food pays for their work.
Not all food comes from a farm. Some people grow tomatoes in a garden. Some catch fish in Lake Michigan. But most food takes many hands. Every meal is a gift of work.

words.d: a plant a farmer grows to sell, like corn or beans

look.title: The Farmer's Year
look.text: Look at the same field four times. Spring: the farmer drives a planter. Brown dirt in rows. Summer: green corn taller than a kid. Fall: a big machine cuts the corn. Winter: the field is white with snow. The farmer fixes her machines in the barn.
look.prompt: When is the farmer working? Is there a season with no work?

check.q: What is a crop?
choices: A plant a farmer grows to sell
check.why: A crop is a plant grown to sell. Corn is a big crop in Illinois.

check.q: Your family buys corn. Who gets some of that money?
choices: The farmer, the driver and the store worker
check.why: Buying food pays for the work of everyone who helped, not just the store.

check.q: Which season shows the farmer picking corn?
check.why: The farmer plants in spring and picks the corn in fall.

review.why: Food is a need. You cannot live without it. A bike and a sticker are wants.

review.q: How do most grown-ups get money?
review.why: People work at jobs. Then they get paid. That is earning.
A bus ride is work someone does for you. That is a service.

review.q: Leo keeps his money in a jar for the bike. What is he doing?
review.why: Saving means keeping money now to use later. Leo is saving for the bike.

review.q: Why can't Leo buy the cone and the bike?
choices: Money runs out, so he must choose
